Extreme competition between stripes and superconductivity in the hole-doped Hubbard model

Ao Chen Email: chenao.phys@gmail.com Affiliation: Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, USA Affiliation: Marcus Center for Theoretical Chemistry, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, USA    Johnnie Gray Affiliation: Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, USA Affiliation: Marcus Center for Theoretical Chemistry, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, USA    Si-Jing Du Affiliation: Division of Engineering and Applied Science, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, USA Affiliation: Marcus Center for Theoretical Chemistry, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, USA    Garnet Kin-Lic Chan Email: gkc1000@gmail.com Affiliation: Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, USA Affiliation: Marcus Center for Theoretical Chemistry, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, USA
October 26, 2026
Abstract

The two-dimensional Hubbard model was originally proposed as the minimal model of uniform dd-wave superconductivity in the cuprate high-temperature superconductors, but recent calculations with relevant parameters in a realistic doping regime have often found other ground states. Further, uncertainty remains over such results due to the intrinsic bias of different computational methods. Here we address this uncertainty through state-of-the-art neural tensor network and neural backflow state simulations, enabled by large-scale GPU computation, that together reach an unprecedented variational accuracy on lattices with up to 1024 sites. At 1/81/8 doping in the pure Hubbard model, as well as with next-nearest-neighbor hopping relevant to the hole-doped cuprates, we reveal a near degeneracy among a low-energy uniform dd-wave state, superconducting stripes, and non-superconducting stripe states on the milli-tt energy scale. Our work rebalances the narrative that the Hubbard model supports a single dominant order in relevant parameter regimes towards a picture of extreme competition between stripes and superconductivity.

I Introduction

The Hubbard model is a paradigmatic model of strongly correlated electrons [4, 69]. Despite its simple form, the two-dimensional (2D) Hubbard model is believed to capture the essential physics of high-temperature superconductivity (SC) [10, 52], and can be realized directly by ultracold fermionic atoms in optical lattices [26, 82, 58, 40]. In the cuprate materials that the Hubbard model aims to describe, uniform dd-wave superconductivity is found at optimal doping, while in certain cuprates other low-temperature orders can also be observed [47, 29]. For example, there is evidence for various unidirectional orders such as spin-density waves (SDW), charge-density waves (CDW), stripes (with intertwined spin and charge modulations), and even more exotic orders such as pair-density waves in several materials at low doping [47, 29], and these have been argued to either coexist with, be intertwined with, or compete with superconductivity.

Numerical studies of the hole-doped Hubbard model find different ordered ground states at the same point in the phase diagram. We summarize some recent results here, which can be roughly categorized as shown in Fig. 1(a). For the pure Hubbard model, multiple methods such as the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG), projected entangled pair states (PEPS), density matrix embedding theory (DMET), constrained-path (CP-) and variational (V) auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC), and neural network backflow (NNBF) states all find a filled stripe at U=8U=8 and 1/81/8 doping [95, 68, 80, 55, 73], while Ref. [80] also saw an energetically competitive uniform dd-wave superconducting state at that point. With a next-nearest-neighbor hopping t′≈−0.2t^{\prime}\approx-0.2 relevant to the hole-doped cuprates [3, 66], the conclusions are more varied. Again at 1/81/8 doping, robust superconductivity coexisting with partially filled stripes has been reported in a DMRG/CP-AFQMC study [91] and a neural Pfaffian study [73], whereas other simulations using infinite PEPS [67] and other NNBF states [36, 35] have found non-superconducting stripes, while a DMRG study found only a CDW with short-range pairing [46].

The diversity of observations can be traced to the sensitivity of the Hubbard model ground state to biases of the numerical simulations. While it is possible to make progress through the consensus of different techniques which individually have uncertainties larger than the energy scale of competing orders—for example, the study of stripes in Ref. [95] involved an energy spread across methods of roughly 0.010.01 tt, larger than the energy difference between competing stripe wavelengths—the only way to eliminate this uncertainty is to improve the absolute accuracy of the simulations. To this end, we employ variational wavefunctions that can in principle be improved to arbitrary accuracy and that in practice we push to the precision of a few milli-tt on lattices with up to 1024 sites. We employ two variants of NNBF [57], which have recently demonstrated high accuracy in Hubbard model studies [36, 17, 73, 56, 35, 72], as well as a newly introduced neural tensor network state [23], namely the neural-network fermionic PEPS (NN-fPEPS). The rationale for using multiple variational forms is that each relies on an underlying fermionic ansatz that may impose a bias in the calculation. The Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer (BCS) [7] and Pfaffian NNBF states have been argued to favor paired states [88], while the fermionic PEPS (fPEPS) [20, 50, 62, 30] underlying the NN-fPEPS wavefunction favors low entanglement, a very different starting point. In each case, through intensive optimization of the underlying computational infrastructure, as well as through deploying large-scale graphics processing unit (GPU) computation, we push each variational form to the practical limits of accuracy. As we shall detail below, this leads to new findings and insights regarding the ground-state order in the hole-doped Hubbard model.

II Hubbard model and competing orders

The Hamiltonian of the Hubbard model is

H=−t∑⟨i,j⟩,σ(ci​σ†cj​σ+H.c.)−t′∑⟨⟨i,j⟩⟩,σ(ci​σ†cj​σ+H.c.)+U∑ini↑ni↓,H=-t\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle,\sigma}\left(c^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}c_{j\sigma}+\mathrm{H.c.}\right)-t^{\prime}\sum_{\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle,\sigma}\left(c^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}c_{j\sigma}+\mathrm{H.c.}\right)+U\sum_{i}n_{i\uparrow}n_{i\downarrow}, (1)

where ci​σ†c^{\dagger}_{i\sigma} (ci​σc_{i\sigma}) creates (annihilates) an electron with spin σ∈{↑,↓}\sigma\in\{\uparrow,\downarrow\} on site ii, ni​σ=ci​σ†​ci​σn_{i\sigma}=c^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}c_{i\sigma}, ⟨i,j⟩\langle i,j\rangle and ⟨⟨i,j⟩⟩\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle denote nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor bonds with hopping amplitudes tt and t′t^{\prime}, H.c. denotes the Hermitian conjugate, and UU is the on-site repulsion. In this work, we take t=1t=1 as the unit of energy and focus on square lattices of N=L×LN=L\times L sites with periodic boundary conditions (PBC) at 1/81/8 hole doping and U=8U=8, for which there have been many recent studies [95, 68, 80, 91, 73, 36, 35, 72, 88].

We characterize the ground state by two order parameters, the dd-wave pairing ΔSC2\Delta_{\mathrm{SC}}^{2} and the stripe order Mstr2M^{2}_{\mathrm{str}}, which compete in this regime. The pairing order parameter is extracted from the long-distance behavior of the pair-pair correlation function

Cp​(r)=⟨Δ0†​Δr⟩−𝒩0,r,Δr†=14​∑ηhη2​(cr↑†​cr+η,↓†−cr↓†​cr+η,↑†),\begin{split}C_{p}(r)&=\langle\Delta^{\dagger}_{0}\Delta_{r}\rangle-\mathcal{N}_{0,r}\,,\\ \Delta^{\dagger}_{r}&=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{\eta}\frac{h_{\eta}}{\sqrt{2}}\left(c^{\dagger}_{r\uparrow}c^{\dagger}_{r+\eta,\downarrow}-c^{\dagger}_{r\downarrow}c^{\dagger}_{r+\eta,\uparrow}\right)\,,\end{split} (2)

where rr labels lattice sites, η\eta runs over the four nearest-neighbor vectors, the form factor hη=+1h_{\eta}=+1 (−1-1) on horizontal (vertical) bonds selects the dx2−y2d_{x^{2}-y^{2}} channel in the convention of Refs. [68, 91, 72], and 𝒩0,r\mathcal{N}_{0,r} removes the disconnected normal-state contribution, namely the products of one-body correlators ⟨c†​c⟩​⟨c†​c⟩\langle c^{\dagger}c\rangle\langle c^{\dagger}c\rangle in the Wick decomposition of ⟨Δ0†​Δr⟩\langle\Delta^{\dagger}_{0}\Delta_{r}\rangle [73]. The dd-wave order parameter is

ΔSC2=1ℳ​∑|r|≥rmaxCp​(r),\Delta_{\mathrm{SC}}^{2}=\frac{1}{\mathcal{M}}\sum_{|r|\geq r_{\max}}C_{p}(r), (3)

which averages Cp​(r)C_{p}(r) over the ℳ\mathcal{M} vectors with |r|≥rmax|r|\geq r_{\max}, where rmaxr_{\max} is half the largest distance on the PBC lattice [72]. The stripe order parameter is defined through the spin structure factor S⁡(k)=∑rei​k⋅r​⟨𝑺0⋅𝑺r⟩S(k)=\sum_{r}e^{ik\cdot r}\langle\bm{S}_{0}\cdot\bm{S}_{r}\rangle as

Mstr2=14​N​∑α=14S⁡(kα),M^{2}_{\mathrm{str}}=\frac{1}{4N}\sum_{\alpha=1}^{4}S(k_{\alpha})\,, (4)

where 𝑺r\bm{S}_{r} is the spin operator at site rr and kα∈{(π±q,π),(π,π±q)}k_{\alpha}\in\{(\pi\pm q,\pi),(\pi,\pi\pm q)\} are the four peak wavevectors of the stripe order [88]. Apart from the SDW represented by Mstr2M^{2}_{\mathrm{str}}, the stripes also carry a CDW, which coexists with the SDW but appears to be much weaker in our calculations, and is discussed in Sec. VIII of the Supplementary Materials (SM) [1].

The two order parameters can be used to distinguish three candidate ground states, namely the stripe state with Mstr2>0M^{2}_{\mathrm{str}}>0 and ΔSC2=0\Delta^{2}_{\mathrm{SC}}=0, the uniform dd-wave superconductor with ΔSC2>0\Delta^{2}_{\mathrm{SC}}>0 and Mstr2=0M^{2}_{\mathrm{str}}=0, and a striped dd-wave superconductor where both orders are nonzero. Both order parameters must be extrapolated to the thermodynamic limit (TDL). Since each of them breaks a continuous symmetry, they are associated with gapless modes, such as the phase mode of the superconductor and the spin waves of the stripe, which make correlations approach their long-distance value with a correction ∝1/|r|\propto 1/|r|, as in the Heisenberg antiferromagnet [74]. Hence the leading finite-size corrections to ΔSC2\Delta^{2}_{\mathrm{SC}} and Mstr2M^{2}_{\mathrm{str}} are linear in 1/L1/L, and we extrapolate both by straight lines in 1/L1/L. This linear form of Mstr2M^{2}_{\mathrm{str}} against 1/L1/L assumes long-range order. In a state without stripe order, the spin correlations decay over a finite correlation length ξ\xi, so that for L≫ξL\gg\xi the structure factor S⁡(kα)S(k_{\alpha}) no longer grows with the system size and Mstr2∝1/N=1/L2M^{2}_{\mathrm{str}}\propto 1/N=1/L^{2}. We therefore extrapolate the stripe order of states whose S⁡(kα)S(k_{\alpha}) saturates with the size by Mstr2=a+b/L2M^{2}_{\mathrm{str}}=a+b/L^{2}. We evaluate these orders for the three types of wavefunctions introduced in Sec. III, for the pure Hubbard model at t′=0t^{\prime}=0 (Sec. IV.1) and for the tt–t′t^{\prime} Hubbard model at t′=−0.2t^{\prime}=-0.2 (Sec. IV.2).

III Neural and tensor network wavefunctions

In variational Monte Carlo (VMC) simulations [59, 9] of the Hubbard model with neural quantum states (NQS) [13], the variational state is usually expanded in the occupation basis as |Ψ⟩=∑nψ⁡(n)​|n⟩|\Psi\rangle=\sum_{n}\psi(n)|n\rangle, where the configuration space of each site is ni∈{0,↑,↓,↑↓}n_{i}\in\{0,\uparrow,\downarrow,\uparrow\downarrow\}. The NNBF wavefunctions we use are based on the symmetry-preserving backflow pairing state of Ref. [72]. We refer to the specific pairing form in Ref. [72] as the BCS backflow state, and we further generalize it to a Pfaffian pairing form [11, 5, 6], the Pfaffian backflow state, which allows for general orbital coefficients and pairing among the NeN_{e} electrons. Its amplitude is

ψPf​-​BF​(n)=pf⁡[n⋆f⁡(n)⋆n],fi​jσ​σ′​(n)=pi​j​∑α=1dWi−j,ασ​σ′​yi​ασ​(n)​yj​ασ′​(n),\psi_{\mathrm{Pf\text{-}BF}}(n)=\operatorname{pf}\big[n\star f(n)\star n\big],\qquad f^{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}_{ij}(n)=p_{ij}\sum_{\alpha=1}^{d}W^{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}_{i-j,\alpha}\,y^{\sigma}_{i\alpha}(n)\,y^{\sigma^{\prime}}_{j\alpha}(n), (5)

where f⁡(n)f(n) is an antisymmetric 2​N×2​N2N\times 2N pairing matrix whose element fi​jσ​σ′​(n)f^{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}_{ij}(n) connects the spin-orbitals (i,σ)(i,\sigma) and (j,σ′)(j,\sigma^{\prime}), and n⋆f⁡(n)⋆nn\star f(n)\star n denotes its Ne×NeN_{e}\times N_{e} submatrix obtained by retaining only the rows and columns of occupied spin-orbitals. The backflow features yiσ​(n)y^{\sigma}_{i}(n) are dd-dimensional vectors generated by a residual convolutional neural network (CNN) detailed in SM Sec. I [1], with y↑y^{\uparrow} and y↓y^{\downarrow} given by the two halves of its output channels, and pi​j∝e−λ​d​(i,j)p_{ij}\propto e^{-\lambda d(i,j)} is a normalized envelope that decays with the distance d⁡(i,j)d(i,j) between the two sites at a trainable rate λ\lambda. The pairing weights Wi−j,ασ​σ′W^{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}_{i-j,\alpha} depend only on the displacement i−ji-j, so ψPf​-​BF​(n)\psi_{\mathrm{Pf\text{-}BF}}(n) is translation invariant by construction without any symmetry projection, and W−rσ′​σ=−Wrσ​σ′W^{\sigma^{\prime}\sigma}_{-r}=-W^{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}_{r} so that f⁡(n)f(n) is exactly antisymmetric for the symmetric envelope pi​j=pj​ip_{ij}=p_{ji}.

The BCS backflow state is a special case of the Pfaffian backflow state in Eq. (5) with same-spin weights W↑⁣↑=W↓⁣↓=0W^{\uparrow\uparrow}=W^{\downarrow\downarrow}=0. The pairing is then restricted to opposite spins and the Pfaffian reduces to a determinant up to a configuration-independent sign,

ψBCS​-​BF​(n)=det[n↑⋆f↑⁣↓​(n)⋆n↓],\psi_{\mathrm{BCS\text{-}BF}}(n)=\det\big[n_{\uparrow}\star f^{\uparrow\downarrow}(n)\star n_{\downarrow}\big], (6)

where n↑⋆f↑⁣↓​(n)⋆n↓n_{\uparrow}\star f^{\uparrow\downarrow}(n)\star n_{\downarrow} retains the rows of occupied spin-up sites and the columns of occupied spin-down sites of the N×NN\times N block f↑⁣↓​(n)f^{\uparrow\downarrow}(n). The two forms share the same network architecture, and the Pfaffian backflow only adds the same-spin weights. In our reimplementation of the BCS backflow, the Transformer backbone of Ref. [72] is replaced by the same residual CNN.

Our NN-fPEPS is instead built on the fPEPS [20, 50, 62], whose amplitude is given by

ψfPEPS​(n)=∑{α}∏iTni,{αi}[i],\psi_{\mathrm{fPEPS}}(n)=\sum_{\{\alpha\}}\prod_{i}T^{[i]}_{n_{i},\{\alpha_{i}\}}, (7)

where T[i]T^{[i]} is the local tensor at site ii, the subscript nin_{i} gives the physical index slice of the tensor at the local configuration, and {αi}\{\alpha_{i}\} denotes the set of its four virtual indices of bond dimension DD, each shared with a nearest neighbor and traced out by the sum over all virtual indices {α}\{\alpha\}. The tensors are ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-graded such that the contraction automatically generates the minus signs required by fermionic anticommutation [20, 50, 62, 30]. Variational fPEPS, optimized either by simple update or by gradient optimization, have previously been shown to deliver good accuracy at large DD in simulations of the Hubbard model [55]. Below we will use variational fPEPS, with PBC and bond dimension extrapolation, to give an independent estimate of the exact ground-state energy on the 16×1616\times 16 lattice at t′=0t^{\prime}=0 (see SM Sec. VI [1] for details on the pure fPEPS PBC contraction and energy evaluation strategy).

Building on Ref. [23], which introduced a neural parametrization (neuralization) of tensor networks [19, 23, 27] for fermions, we promote the fPEPS to an NN-fPEPS by generating all local tensors with a neural network, and the amplitude becomes

ψNN-fPEPS​(n)=∑{α}∏iTni,{αi}[i]​(n).\psi_{\text{NN-fPEPS}}(n)=\sum_{\{\alpha\}}\prod_{i}T^{[i]}_{n_{i},\{\alpha_{i}\}}(n). (8)

As in the backflow form, the configuration nn enters the amplitude in two distinct ways. The argument (n)(n) indicates that the tensor elements are generated by the neural network from the global configuration, while the subscript nin_{i} slices the physical index of each tensor in the contraction, as in Eq. (7) and in analogy with the selection of occupied spin-orbitals by n⋆f⁡(n)⋆nn\star f(n)\star n in Eq. (5). The NN-fPEPS architecture is illustrated in Fig. 2(a), and, as in our backflow states, the tensors are generated by a residual CNN (SM Sec. I [1]).

The tensor contraction in Eq. (8) is performed approximately by the higher-order tensor renormalization group (HOTRG) [90, 44], which repeatedly merges pairs of adjacent rows, compresses the doubled bonds back to dimension χ\chi by applying oblique projectors, and is naturally compatible with PBC (SM Sec. II [1]). By keeping the same (set of) contraction path(s) for every configuration nn, the approximate HOTRG contraction ensures strict variationality [54] for any D,χD,\chi, and can be easily parallelized [24]. Its time complexity per amplitude is 𝒪⁡(N​χ7)\mathcal{O}(N\chi^{7}), or 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N) at fixed DD and χ\chi. To avoid the high cost of large DD and χ\chi, we choose D=χ=4D=\chi=4 throughout this work and rely on the neural network rather than the tensor network to increase the expressivity. To further restore the strict translation symmetry [72] broken by HOTRG, we express ψNN-fPEPS​(n)\psi_{\text{NN-fPEPS}}(n) as a superposition of a set of contraction paths, which leads to a slightly higher computational complexity of 𝒪⁡(N​log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(N\log N) (SM Sec. III [1]). The NN-fPEPS thus avoids the 𝒪⁡(N3)\mathcal{O}(N^{3}) cost of the Pfaffian and the determinant in the backflow calculations at large system sizes.

The NN-fPEPS and the backflow wavefunctions retain different inductive biases arising from how the fermionic sign structure is enforced, as illustrated in Fig. 1(b). The BCS and Pfaffian backflow states capture pairing through the mean-field wavefunction and have been shown to reach high accuracy if the ground state is indeed a BCS superconductor [17, 72]. Empirically, however, it has been argued that these reference forms bias the state toward superconductivity [88]. In addition, Sec. IV includes the determinant backflow state (ACE) of Ref. [35], which potentially favors stripes over superconductivity [88]. The fPEPS in the NN-fPEPS, in contrast to backflow wavefunctions, favors locally entangled (area-law) ground states [85, 25]. A priori, this feature favors neither stripes nor superconductivity, although specific stripe or superconducting states may carry different amounts of entanglement.

Our simulations are implemented in Quantax [16], which is built on Jax [12] and Equinox [48], and the fPEPS contraction relies on quimb [33, 32] and symmray [34, 30]. In Fig. 2(b), we illustrate the techniques used in our VMC optimization. All parts of the computational graph have been intensively optimized to achieve high throughput on GPUs, including custom kernels for the HOTRG contraction and for the batched determinants and Pfaffians [18]. Several symmetries, including mirror reflections and spin inversion, are imposed by a symmetry projection for better accuracy (SM Sec. III [1]). During the VMC optimization, the variational parameters are trained by an adaptive moment stochastic reconfiguration (AdamSR) optimizer, which combines Adam [49] with common optimizers for NQS [78, 79, 15, 71, 31, 36] for better efficiency and stability. Apart from the common Cholesky solver, we further utilize the iterative least-squares minimal residual (LSMR) linear solver [28] in AdamSR to achieve efficient parallelization on up to 1024 GPUs. The optimizers and solvers are detailed in SM Sec. IV [1], and a careful analysis of the time cost is included in SM Sec. V [1]. Unless otherwise specified, all simulations are performed with 32-bit floating-point (FP32) precision and TensorFloat-32 (TF32) tensor cores for convolutions and matrix multiplications.

IV Results

We now compare the results of the three classes of wavefunctions, namely the BCS backflow state, the Pfaffian backflow state, and the NN-fPEPS, at 1/81/8 doping and U=8U=8, first at t′=0t^{\prime}=0 and then at t′=−0.2t^{\prime}=-0.2. The variational energies and variances of all our states before and after symmetry projection, together with those of previous studies, are listed in SM Sec. VII [1]. The real-space spin, charge, and pair-pair correlation functions of all symmetry-projected states are shown in SM Sec. VIII [1].

IV.1 Pure Hubbard model

We begin with the pure Hubbard model at t′=0t^{\prime}=0 and 1/81/8 doping, where the physics has been more extensively studied than at t′=−0.2t^{\prime}=-0.2. As presented in Fig. 3(a), we reach the lowest variational energies reported so far on both the 16×1616\times 16 and 32×3232\times 32 PBC lattices, below those of the convolutional determinant backflow forms used in ACE and SCALE [35], of the hidden fermion Pfaffian state (HFPS) [73], and of the VAFQMC stripe state [80, 89] listed in SM Sec. VII [1]. On the 16×1616\times 16 lattice, extrapolating a pure fPEPS simple-update calculation with PBC gives an estimated exact energy of E/N=−0.7602​(14)E/N=-0.7602(14) (SM Sec. VI [1]), shown in Fig. 3(a). The energies of all our variational wavefunctions lie within 0.0020.002 tt per site (0.3%0.3\%) of this estimate, and the lowest one (BCS backflow) lies 0.00140.0014 tt above it. This accuracy is consistent with that of the NN-fPEPS on the small 16×416\times 4 lattice, where an accurate benchmark energy is known (SM Sec. VII [1]).

In Fig. 3(b), the pair-pair correlations of the BCS and Pfaffian backflow states saturate at nearly the same plateau at long distances, Cp≈1.3×10−3C_{p}\approx 1.3\times 10^{-3}, which signals long-range superconducting correlations. The NN-fPEPS and the determinant backflow state instead show exponentially decaying correlations, as expected for a pure stripe without pairing, which is also the state found in the large-DD fPEPS calculation. These ansatzes therefore converge to two qualitatively different competing states, a superconductor and a stripe. As indicated by the energies in Fig. 3(a), the NN-fPEPS energy lies below that of the Pfaffian backflow state but slightly above that of the BCS backflow state on the 16×1616\times 16 lattice, by 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} tt per site, while on the 32×3232\times 32 lattice its energy is clearly lower than that of the BCS backflow state, by 6×10−46\times 10^{-4} tt per site. This trend indicates that the NN-fPEPS captures the striped ground state of large lattices, whereas the superconducting state seen in the BCS and Pfaffian backflow ansatzes is a competing state at higher energy in the TDL.

The order parameters are further analyzed in Fig. 3(c) as a function of lattice size. On the 16×1616\times 16 lattice, the BCS backflow state has ΔSC2=0.00135​(1)\Delta^{2}_{\mathrm{SC}}=0.00135(1) and Mstr2=0.009415​(3)M^{2}_{\mathrm{str}}=0.009415(3), the weakest stripe order among the three states. Its pairing strength exceeds even that of the BCS backflow result at t′=−0.2t^{\prime}=-0.2 (Sec. IV.2), where superconductivity has been previously reported and argued to be stronger than at t′=0t^{\prime}=0. On the 32×3232\times 32 lattice its pairing is essentially unchanged, ΔSC2=0.00141​(3)\Delta^{2}_{\mathrm{SC}}=0.00141(3), and extrapolated linearly in 1/L1/L it stays finite with ΔSC2=0.00146​(6)\Delta^{2}_{\mathrm{SC}}=0.00146(6), i.e., ΔSC=0.0382​(8)\Delta_{\mathrm{SC}}=0.0382(8). Its stripe order, in contrast, drops by a factor of 4.44.4 to Mstr2=0.002145​(4)M^{2}_{\mathrm{str}}=0.002145(4), and its extrapolation in 1/L21/L^{2} gives Mstr2=−0.0003M^{2}_{\mathrm{str}}=-0.0003, consistent with a vanishing stripe order in the TDL. The BCS backflow wavefunction thus describes a uniform dd-wave superconductor in the TDL, and its weak stripe signal on finite lattices is a finite-size effect. Although the Pfaffian backflow state has more variational freedom, it behaves similarly, and its order parameters are comparable to those obtained by the BCS backflow state on the 16×1616\times 16 lattice.

The NN-fPEPS, in contrast, gives a filled stripe with q=π/8q=\pi/8, i.e., a spin period of 1616, with the extrapolated stripe order Mstr2=0.0082M^{2}_{\mathrm{str}}=0.0082, while its exponentially decaying pair-pair correlation is consistent with vanishing superconducting order. The NN-fPEPS and the BCS backflow solutions therefore realize two distinct candidate states in the TDL, a filled stripe without pairing as the ground state and a uniform dd-wave superconductor as a low-energy competing state. Our striped ground state agrees with the filled stripes without superconductivity found by a broad range of previous studies at U=8U=8 and 1/81/8 doping [95, 68, 80, 73]. The uniform dd-wave superconductor expressed by the backflow states has not been commonly seen in recent numerical work, but its low energy matches the energetically competitive uniform dd-wave state that VAFQMC finds within 0.0010.001 tt per site of the stripe [80]. This is a much lower energy scale of competition than seen in early DMET and infinite PEPS studies, which stabilized a uniform dd-wave state in constrained 2×22\times 2 unit cells at energies of about 0.010.01 tt per site above the stripe [95]. This indicates the importance of long-range fluctuations in stabilizing the uniform dd-wave state. We note that in the closely related tt–JJ model, a uniform dd-wave state has likewise been reported to be among the low-energy states [21, 92].

IV.2 tt–t′t^{\prime} Hubbard model

We now apply a similar analysis to the tt–t′t^{\prime} Hubbard model at t′=−0.2t^{\prime}=-0.2 and 1/81/8 doping, shown in Fig. 4. For this model, we take the BCS backflow state energies from the recent study in Ref. [72] and reanalyze the order parameters of these states. As presented in Fig. 4(a), our wavefunctions again reach the lowest variational energies reported so far, and the Pfaffian backflow state achieves the lowest energies on all lattice sizes from 16×1616\times 16 to 32×3232\times 32. Unlike at t′=0t^{\prime}=0, the pair-pair correlations of the NN-fPEPS, BCS backflow, and Pfaffian backflow states in Fig. 4(b) saturate at a finite plateau, so all three states carry superconducting correlations on finite lattices. While their short-distance correlations are similar in magnitude, the plateau of the BCS backflow state is 2.42.4 times higher than that of the Pfaffian backflow state and 4.64.6 times higher than that of the NN-fPEPS. In contrast, the determinant backflow state has vanishing long-range dd-wave pairing. The ansatzes differ even more in the strength of their stripe order, shown in Fig. 4(c). For the BCS backflow state, the structure factor peaks at q=π/6q=\pi/6 on both the 12×1212\times 12 and 24×2424\times 24 lattices, where Mstr2=0.0125M^{2}_{\mathrm{str}}=0.0125 and 0.00300.0030, the latter being already 3.33.3 times weaker than the 0.00998​(1)0.00998(1) order of the Pfaffian backflow on the same lattice. Its peak S⁡(kα)S(k_{\alpha}) hardly changes between the two sizes, so the spin correlations are short-ranged, and the extrapolation in 1/L21/L^{2} gives Mstr2=−0.0001M^{2}_{\mathrm{str}}=-0.0001. We note that our extrapolation, which starts from the small 12×1212\times 12 lattice, is subject to strong finite-size effects and may thus not be entirely reliable. Nevertheless, since the stripe order is much weaker than that of the other two variational states, we regard the BCS backflow state as evidence of a (nearly) uniform low-energy state in the TDL. The Pfaffian backflow state and the NN-fPEPS instead form a pronounced stripe order with q=π/4q=\pi/4, i.e., a spin period of 88, whose Mstr2M^{2}_{\mathrm{str}} extrapolates to 0.01000.0100 for the NN-fPEPS and 0.00700.0070 for the Pfaffian backflow, indicating a striped state in the TDL. Similarly, the determinant backflow state also shows a strong stripe order with q=π/4q=\pi/4 [35]. Independent of this consensus between these different ansatzes, the low energy achieved by the Pfaffian backflow wavefunction lends further support to a non-uniform ground state in the TDL.

The extrapolation of the superconducting pairing order is shown in Fig. 4(c). Extrapolating ΔSC2\Delta^{2}_{\mathrm{SC}}, we find that the BCS backflow state of Ref. [72] retains a sizable ΔSC=0.019​(4)\Delta_{\mathrm{SC}}=0.019(4) in the TDL, slightly below the value 0.022​(1)0.022(1) obtained in Ref. [72] by extrapolating ΔSC\Delta_{\mathrm{SC}} itself. Since, as discussed above, its stripe order is very weak (and potentially vanishes in a TDL extrapolation), we reinterpret this as evidence of a (nearly) uniform dd-wave superconducting low-energy state in the TDL, rather than the striped superconducting state originally discussed in Ref. [72]. The Pfaffian backflow state and the NN-fPEPS give much weaker pairing in the TDL. For the NN-fPEPS, the linear fit through the 16×1616\times 16 and 32×3232\times 32 lattices yields ΔSC=0.007​(2)\Delta_{\mathrm{SC}}=0.007(2). For the Pfaffian backflow, the result depends on the fit. The linear 1/L1/L fit over L=16L=16, 2424, and 3232 in Fig. 4(c) gives ΔSC\Delta_{\mathrm{SC}} consistent with zero, with an upper bound of 0.0060.006 at one standard deviation. A fit through the 24×2424\times 24 and 32×3232\times 32 lattices alone gives a small but finite ΔSC=0.010​(3)\Delta_{\mathrm{SC}}=0.010(3). Either way, the extrapolated pairing gives ΔSC≲0.010\Delta_{\mathrm{SC}}\lesssim 0.010, i.e., a striped ground state with weak or absent superconductivity. This stands in contrast to the striped superconducting ground state with a longer wavelength and a larger ΔSC=0.017​(3)\Delta_{\mathrm{SC}}=0.017(3) proposed by CP-AFQMC [91]. Taken together, these results thus point to stripes with weaker or absent superconductivity, stripes with robust superconductivity, and a uniform dd-wave state, all existing in competition near the ground state.

V Conclusion and outlook

We have studied the competition between stripes and superconductivity in the hole-doped Hubbard model with U=8U=8 and 1/81/8 doping using three classes of variational states: BCS backflow states, Pfaffian backflow states, and NN-fPEPS. On the lattices considered, from 16×1616\times 16 up to 32×3232\times 32 sites, the accuracy of our variational energies exceeds that of all prior studies of this model. In the pure Hubbard model at t′=0t^{\prime}=0, our work lends further support to the long-standing proposal of a non-superconducting striped ground state [95, 68]. At t′=−0.2t^{\prime}=-0.2, we find evidence for weak or vanishing superconductivity with strong stripe order in the ground state, which is different from recent studies that saw a robust dd-wave striped superconducting ground state [91, 73], although the latter could still represent a different low-lying state [95]. Both with and without t′t^{\prime}, we find at this doping that an ordered stripe suppresses superconductivity, so that the ground state is either not superconducting or only weakly superconducting. However, at both values of t′t^{\prime}, we also find a strongly superconducting uniform dd-wave state nearby on a milli-tt energy scale, resembling the proposal in Ref. [80].

Beyond the physical findings, our work highlights and advances two aspects of current simulation methodology. First, despite being highly parametrized, modern neural wavefunctions retain biases that are not overcome in training. They must therefore be cross-validated using different techniques, as done here, in order to identify the qualitative nature of the ground state. Second, the neural tensor networks, improved here from Ref. [23], now offer state-of-the-art performance in large-scale simulations of a strongly correlated electron system, without using a mean-field reference. Taken together, these two aspects suggest a new framework where neural wavefunctions with different fermionic references are combined for reliable studies.

We now discuss prospects for future definitive simulations of superconductivity in the Hubbard model ground state. A finite lattice can resolve the pairing only once the gap Δ\Delta exceeds the mean spacing of the single-particle levels, roughly the bandwidth 8​t8t of the square lattice divided by NN, which requires N≳8​t/ΔN\gtrsim 8t/\Delta. For ΔSC∼0.02\Delta_{\mathrm{SC}}\sim 0.02 comparable to the uniform dd-wave superconductors in this work and previous estimates at t′=−0.2t^{\prime}=-0.2 [72, 91], and taking Δ≈ΔSC​t\Delta\approx\Delta_{\mathrm{SC}}t from BCS theory, eliminating the finite-size effects on the pairing requires N≳400N\gtrsim 400 sites, a number that is expected to be further reduced in the strong-coupling limit [94, 65]. Running on up to 10241024 GPUs, we simulated N≈1000N\approx 1000 sites and thus have reached a regime where finite-size errors arguably no longer dominate the physics and TDL extrapolation is reliable. On the other hand, the condensation energy relative to a hypothetical paramagnetic normal state is estimated to be <10−3<10^{-3} tt [38]. If the mechanism driving superconductivity is related to the formation of the striped state, we may expect a competing stripe state to gain some of this energy, and thus to compete with the superconducting state at the milli-tt scale or below, which is what we see in our work. The overall picture is that stripes, striped superconductivity, and uniform superconductivity all exist in extreme competition in the hole-doped Hubbard model, and resolving this competition requires an extreme level of accuracy. Our work presents a concrete step in this direction.

I Neural network architecture

Both the neural-network fermionic projected entangled pair state (NN-fPEPS) and the Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer (BCS) and Pfaffian backflow states (here, we use ‘backflows’ for short) generate their configuration-dependent features with a residual convolutional neural network (CNN), sketched in Fig. S1 with its settings in Table S1. A learned embedding maps the local state of each site to a CC-dimensional vector xi=enix_{i}=e_{n_{i}}, with the same table ee on every site to preserve translation symmetry, followed by pre-activation residual blocks [41, 42]. The two networks differ in the residual block, which is the bottleneck block in the NN-fPEPS and the normal block in the backflows. Since the convolutions share their weights across sites, the same network applies to every system size, enabling weight transfer from small to large lattices.

The network of the NN-fPEPS maps nn to the elements of all local tensors T[i]​(n)T^{[i]}(n). A ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-graded site tensor has a physical index of dimension 44, with {|0⟩,|↑↓⟩}\{|0\rangle,|{\uparrow\downarrow}\rangle\} even and {|↑⟩,|↓⟩}\{|{\uparrow}\rangle,|{\downarrow}\rangle\} odd, and four virtual indices of dimension DD, each with D/2D/2 even and D/2D/2 odd basis states. Parity conservation removes half of its 4​D44D^{4} elements, so the network outputs C=2​D4C=2D^{4} real channels per site, C=512C=512 at the bond dimension D=4D=4 used in this work. Slicing the physical index at nin_{i} gives the tensors contracted by the higher-order tensor renormalization group (HOTRG) of Sec. II. This width is fixed by DD and far wider than the networks typically used in variational Monte Carlo (VMC), so the NN-fPEPS stacks bottleneck blocks [41]. A residual block at full width would carry 9​C2≈2.4×1069C^{2}\approx 2.4\times 10^{6} weights in its 3×33\times 3 convolution alone, 8.58.5 times the parameters and floating-point operations (FLOP) of a bottleneck block. The width C=64C=64 of the backflows is a free choice rather than being fixed by the bond dimension DD, so they need no bottleneck.

II HOTRG contraction

A HOTRG overview

For a given configuration nn, the amplitude ψNN-fPEPS​(n)\psi_{\text{NN-fPEPS}}(n) is the contraction of a single-layer Lx×LyL_{x}\times L_{y} fermionic projected entangled pair state (fPEPS) of four-leg tensors on a torus. All tensors are ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-graded fermionic arrays [20, 50, 62], so every operation acts blockwise on the two fermion-parity sectors of each index and generates the fermionic signs automatically.

We contract the network by HOTRG steps [90, 44] along yy (Fig. S2), a fixed path that suits the regular torus and the batched evaluation of Monte Carlo samples better than the hyperoptimized schemes designed for arbitrary geometries [32]. The coarse-graining stops at Ly=4L_{y}=4, a width that allows for exact contraction at D=χ=4D=\chi=4, and the four tensors of each remaining column are contracted exactly into a transfer matrix MiM_{i} of dimension χ4=256\chi^{4}=256. The exact contraction of these transfer matrices gives

ψ(n)=tr(M1M2⋯MLx).\psi(n)=\mathrm{tr}\left(M_{1}M_{2}\cdots M_{L_{x}}\right). (S1)

At D=χD=\chi each HOTRG step costs 𝒪⁡(χ7)\mathcal{O}(\chi^{7}) per merged pair and the lattice halves at every step, so the contraction costs 𝒪⁡(N​χ7)\mathcal{O}(N\chi^{7}) for N=Lx​LyN=L_{x}L_{y} sites. Because χ\chi is fixed and no singular-value cutoff is applied, every configuration follows the same sequence of dense linear algebra with static shapes, which is evaluated for a whole Monte Carlo batch in one call on the graphics processing unit (GPU) and keeps the sampled energy strictly variational [54]. The contraction runs in single precision, with TF32 in the final exact contraction, and gradients are obtained by automatic differentiation.

B HOTRG step

A step merges every pair of yy-adjacent tensors T[i,2​j]T^{[i,2j]} and T[i,2​j+1]T^{[i,2j+1]}, uniformly across the periodic lattice. The merged tensor inherits the xx legs of both parents, and each doubled xx bond is compressed back to dimension χ\chi by a pair of oblique projectors PL​PR≈𝟙P_{L}P_{R}\approx\openone [44]. The projectors on the bond between the coarse sites (i,j)(i,j) and (i+1,j)(i+1,j) are computed from the 2×22\times 2 patch of the two pairs ALA_{L} and ARA_{R} (dashed boxes), with all bond dimensions set to χ\chi,

where PL/R[i,j]P_{L/R}^{[i,j]} are given by Eqs. (S2)–(S5) with AL=A[i,j]A_{L}=A^{[i,j]} and AR=A[i+1,j]A_{R}=A^{[i+1,j]}.

The complexity of each step is summarized in Table S2.

C Implementation

A direct evaluation of Eqs. (S3)–(S5) is not optimal on GPUs. The triangular inverses in Eq. (S5) are ill-conditioned, and dense QR and SVD routines parallelize poorly and complicate automatic differentiation. Following quimb [33], we therefore replace every stage by matrix products, Cholesky factorizations, and Hermitian eigendecompositions, as summarized in Table S2 and described below in the order of the algorithm. All matrices are block diagonal in fermion parity, so each factorization acts on two blocks of half the size, batched together with the doubled bonds and the Monte Carlo samples in a single call. At D=χ=4D=\chi=4 these blocks are only 8×88\times 8, a size at which generic fermionic tensor libraries [34, 30] are bound by memory latency rather than arithmetic. The performance-critical stages therefore run as custom fused GPU kernels, each passing over the tensor data once instead of streaming it through a long chain of small library calls. These kernels were prepared with the assistance of Claude Code, as acknowledged in the main text.

The first stage computes the triangular factors RL/RR_{L/R} of Eq. (S3). The projectors need only these factors and never the isometries QL/RQ_{L/R}, so we use the faster Cholesky QR algorithm instead of a full QR factorization. The factors follow from the Gram matrices ML=AL†​AL=RL†​RLM_{L}=A_{L}^{\dagger}A_{L}=R_{L}^{\dagger}R_{L} and MR=AR​AR†=RR​RR†M_{R}=A_{R}A_{R}^{\dagger}=R_{R}R_{R}^{\dagger}, which are contracted directly as tensor networks of each pair with its own conjugate, so that AL/RA_{L/R} is never formed explicitly. Forming and factorizing the Gram matrices costs 𝒪⁡(χ6)\mathcal{O}(\chi^{6}), compared with 𝒪⁡(χ8)\mathcal{O}(\chi^{8}) for a dense QR factorization of AL/RA_{L/R}. The Cholesky factorization requires a positive-definite input, whereas ML/RM_{L/R} is only positive semidefinite and has the squared condition number of AL/RA_{L/R}. We therefore regularize it by the relative diagonal shift

M→M+ϵ​tr​(M)​𝟙,M\to M+\epsilon\,\mathrm{tr}(M)\,\openone, (S7)

with ϵ=10−4\epsilon=10^{-4}.

The second stage computes the truncated SVD of the core B=RL​RRB=R_{L}R_{R} in Eq. (S4). As the SVD is slow on GPUs, we use the Hermitian eigendecomposition of the Gram matrix of BB,

B†​B=V​Λ​V†,Sχ=Λχ1/2,Uχ=B​Vχ​Sχ−1,B^{\dagger}B=V\Lambda V^{\dagger},\qquad S_{\chi}=\Lambda_{\chi}^{1/2},\qquad U_{\chi}=BV_{\chi}S_{\chi}^{-1}, (S8)

where Λχ\Lambda_{\chi} and VχV_{\chi} contain the χ/2\chi/2 largest eigenpairs of each parity sector. The Gram matrix B†​BB^{\dagger}B is regularized by Eq. (S7) with ϵ=10−6\epsilon=10^{-6}, which keeps the retained singular values away from zero, so that the inverse powers of SχS_{\chi} here and in Eq. (S9) stay well conditioned.

The third stage assembles the projectors. Inserting RL−1=RR​B−1R_{L}^{-1}=R_{R}B^{-1}, RR−1=B−1​RLR_{R}^{-1}=B^{-1}R_{L}, and B−1=V​S−1​U†B^{-1}=VS^{-1}U^{\dagger} into Eq. (S5) gives the robust projectors

PL=RRVχSχ−1/2,PR=Sχ−1/2Uχ†RL.P_{L}=R_{R}V_{\chi}S_{\chi}^{-1/2},\qquad P_{R}=S_{\chi}^{-1/2}U_{\chi}^{\dagger}R_{L}. (S9)

They are mathematically equivalent to Eq. (S5), but the triangular inverses are replaced by matrix products. The only remaining inverse, Sχ−1/2S_{\chi}^{-1/2}, involves only the retained singular values, which the shift above keeps bounded away from zero.

The fourth stage merges each pair A[i,j]A^{[i,j]} with its two neighboring projectors as in Eq. (S6) with a dominant cost of 𝒪⁡(χ7)\mathcal{O}(\chi^{7}), and it runs as a fused kernel.

After the last HOTRG step, the final contraction evaluates Eq. (S1). A fused kernel builds the transfer matrices MiM_{i} directly in their parity-blocked layout. Finally, the VMC optimization differentiates ψ⁡(n)\psi(n) through the entire contraction. The reverse-mode gradient of the eigendecomposition in Eq. (S8) contains denominators 1/(λk−λl)1/(\lambda_{k}-\lambda_{l}) that diverge for nearly degenerate eigenvalues. We replace them by the broadened form (λk−λl)/[(λk−λl)2+ε2](\lambda_{k}-\lambda_{l})/[(\lambda_{k}-\lambda_{l})^{2}+\varepsilon^{2}] with a small ε\varepsilon proportional to the spectral radius [53], which keeps the gradients stable throughout the optimization.

III Symmetry

A Symmetry in fermion systems

Projecting a variational state onto an irreducible representation of the symmetry group GG of the Hamiltonian typically lowers its variational energy [81, 64], but for fermions the permutation of modes generates a sign that has to be tracked explicitly [61, 17]. A symmetry g∈Gg\in G permutes the single-particle modes xx, comprising site and spin, as g^​cx†​g^−1=cg​x†\hat{g}\,c^{\dagger}_{x}\,\hat{g}^{-1}=c^{\dagger}_{gx} with g^​|0⟩=|0⟩\hat{g}|0\rangle=|0\rangle. On the Fock state |n⟩=cx1†⋯cxNe†|0⟩|n\rangle=c^{\dagger}_{x_{1}}\cdots c^{\dagger}_{x_{N_{e}}}|0\rangle with x1<⋯<xNex_{1}<\cdots<x_{N_{e}} in a fixed reference order, it acts as

g^|n⟩=cg​x1†⋯cg​xNe†|0⟩=Π(n,g)|gn⟩,\hat{g}|n\rangle=c^{\dagger}_{gx_{1}}\cdots c^{\dagger}_{gx_{N_{e}}}|0\rangle=\Pi(n,g)\,|gn\rangle\,, (S10)

where Π⁡(n,g)=±1\Pi(n,g)=\pm 1 is the signature of the permutation that sorts g​x1,…,g​xNegx_{1},\ldots,gx_{N_{e}} back into the reference order. On a spinless four-site ring, for instance, 𝒯^1c2†c4†|0⟩=c3†c1†|0⟩=−|1,0,1,0⟩\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{1}c^{\dagger}_{2}c^{\dagger}_{4}|0\rangle=c^{\dagger}_{3}c^{\dagger}_{1}|0\rangle=-|1,0,1,0\rangle, where Π⁡(n,g)=−1\Pi(n,g)=-1. The projection |Ψsymm⟩=|G​|∑g−1⁡ωg∗​g^|​Ψ⟩|\Psi^{\text{symm}}\rangle=|G|^{-1}\sum_{g}\omega^{*}_{g}\,\hat{g}|\Psi\rangle onto the representation with characters ωg\omega_{g} then has the amplitudes

ψsymm​(n)=1|G|​∑g∈GΠ⁡(n,g)​ωg​ψ​(g​n).\psi^{\text{symm}}(n)=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\Pi(n,g)\,\omega_{g}\,\psi(gn)\,. (S11)

We project onto the trivial representation, ωg=1\omega_{g}=1, of the group generated by the NN translations 𝒯t\mathcal{T}_{t} and

P={1,Mx}×{1,My}×{1,Z},P=\{1,M_{x}\}\times\{1,M_{y}\}\times\{1,Z\}\,, (S12)

where Mx:(x,y)↦(−x,y)M_{x}:(x,y)\mapsto(-x,y) and My:(x,y)↦(x,−y)M_{y}:(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y) are the mirrors about the lattice axes and ZZ exchanges the two spin species. Each element of PP costs one more network evaluation and contraction, a size-independent factor of 88.

B Translation symmetry in NN-fPEPS

The circular convolutions make the network translation covariant,

T[r]​(𝒯t​n)=T[r+t]​(n),T^{[r]}(\mathcal{T}_{t}n)=T^{[r+t]}(n), (S13)

so an exact contraction would give translation-symmetric amplitudes. HOTRG merges the fixed pairs (2​j,2​j+1)(2j,2j+1), however, so configurations translated along yy are truncated differently, and ψ\psi of Eq. (S1) keeps only the translation symmetry along xx. We restore it by the zero-momentum projection

ψtrans​(n)=1N​∑tΠ⁡(n,𝒯t)​ψ​(𝒯t​n),\psi^{\text{trans}}(n)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t}\Pi(n,\mathcal{T}_{t})\,\psi(\mathcal{T}_{t}n), (S14)

which naively costs NN contractions, 𝒪⁡(N2​χ7)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}\chi^{7}) per configuration. Instead, the network runs once, since by Eq. (S13) all translated tensor grids are rolls of the same grid, and the HOTRG steps are shared among the translations, as presented in Fig. S3. The kk-th step is evaluated for 2k2^{k} representatives on a lattice of N/2kN/2^{k} tensors, so that

∑k=1log2⁡(Ly/4)2k⏟representatives×𝒪⁡(N​χ7/2k)⏟cost of one step=𝒪⁡(N​χ7​log⁡N),\sum_{k=1}^{\log_{2}(L_{y}/4)}\underbrace{2^{k}}_{\text{representatives}}\times\underbrace{\mathcal{O}\!\left(N\chi^{7}/2^{k}\right)}_{\text{cost of one step}}=\mathcal{O}\!\left(N\chi^{7}\log N\right), (S15)

and the final exact contraction, performed once per representative, does not change this scaling.

The group PP in Eq. (S12) is then applied as an outer loop,

ψsymm​(n)=1|P|​∑p∈PΠ⁡(n,p)​ψtrans​(p​n),\psi^{\text{symm}}(n)=\frac{1}{|P|}\sum_{p\in P}\Pi(n,p)\,\psi^{\text{trans}}(p\,n)\,, (S16)

which realizes Eq. (S11) for the full group. All results are obtained with ψsymm​(n)\psi^{\text{symm}}(n) unless otherwise specified.

IV Optimizer

A AdamSR

 

Algorithm S1. AdamSR

 
1: momentum factors μ=0.95\mu=0.95 and β=0.995\beta=0.995, norm-constrained step size γt\gamma_{t} of Eq. (S18) or Eq. (S19)
2: m0←0m_{0}\leftarrow 0,  v0←0v_{0}\leftarrow 0
3: for t=1,2,…t=1,2,\dots do
4:   sample configurations nsn_{s} from |ψ⁡(n)|2|\psi(n)|^{2} and construct O¯\bar{O} and ϵ¯\bar{\epsilon} in Eq. (S17)
5:   gt←O¯+​ϵ¯g_{t}\leftarrow\bar{O}^{+}\bar{\epsilon} ⊳\triangleright plain MinSR solution
6:   mt←μ​mt−1+(1−μ)​gtm_{t}\leftarrow\mu\,m_{t-1}+(1-\mu)\,g_{t},  m^t←mt/(1−μt)\hat{m}_{t}\leftarrow m_{t}/\left(1-\mu^{t}\right) ⊳\triangleright Adam first moment
7:   vt←β​vt−1+(1−β)​|gt|2v_{t}\leftarrow\beta\,v_{t-1}+(1-\beta)\,|g_{t}|^{2},  v^t←vt/(1−βt)\hat{v}_{t}\leftarrow v_{t}/\left(1-\beta^{t}\right) ⊳\triangleright Adam second moment
8:   Vt←diag​(v^t)1/4+10−8​𝟙V_{t}\leftarrow\mathrm{diag}\big(\hat{v}_{t}\big)^{1/4}+10^{-8}\,\openone ⊳\triangleright diagonal preconditioner
9:   δ​θt←m^t+Vt−1​(O¯​Vt−1)+​(ϵ¯−O¯​m^t)\delta\theta_{t}\leftarrow\hat{m}_{t}+V_{t}^{-1}\big(\bar{O}V_{t}^{-1}\big)^{+}\big(\bar{\epsilon}-\bar{O}\hat{m}_{t}\big) ⊳\triangleright momentum ++ preconditioned correction
10:   θt←θt−1−γt​(∥δ​θt∥)​δ​θt\theta_{t}\leftarrow\theta_{t-1}-\gamma_{t}\big(\lVert\delta\theta_{t}\rVert\big)\,\delta\theta_{t} ⊳\triangleright norm-constrained update
11: end for
 

The variational parameters θ\theta are optimized by stochastic reconfiguration (SR) [78, 79], which realizes imaginary-time evolution projected onto the variational manifold. At every iteration, NsN_{s} configurations nsn_{s} are sampled from |ψ⁡(n)|2|\psi(n)|^{2} by Markov-chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), and the update θ˙\dot{\theta} of the NpN_{p} parameters solves

O¯​θ˙=−ϵ¯,O¯s​k=Ok​(ns)−⟨Ok⟩Ns,ϵ¯s=Eloc​(ns)−⟨Eloc⟩Ns,\bar{O}\,\dot{\theta}=-\bar{\epsilon}\,,\qquad\bar{O}_{sk}=\frac{O_{k}(n_{s})-\left<O_{k}\right>}{\sqrt{N_{s}}}\,,\qquad\bar{\epsilon}_{s}=\frac{E_{\mathrm{loc}}(n_{s})-\left<E_{\mathrm{loc}}\right>}{\sqrt{N_{s}}}\,, (S17)

with Ok​(n)=∂ln⁡ψ⁡(n)/∂θkO_{k}(n)=\partial\ln\psi(n)/\partial\theta_{k}, the local energy Eloc​(n)=∑n′⟨n|H|n′⟩​ψ​(n′)/ψ⁡(n)E_{\mathrm{loc}}(n)=\sum_{n^{\prime}}\left<n|H|n^{\prime}\right>\psi(n^{\prime})/\psi(n), and ⟨⋅⟩\left<\,\cdot\,\right> the sample average.

Since Ns≪NpN_{s}\ll N_{p}, Eq. (S17) is underdetermined and has infinitely many solutions. This freedom lets the solver carry the first and second moments of the update, which accelerate and stabilize first-order optimizers such as Adam [49], without giving up the SR equation. In previous works, SPRING [31] incorporates the first moment, and MARCH [36] further includes the second moment. In this work, we introduce the adaptive moment stochastic reconfiguration (AdamSR) as presented in Algorithm A, which keeps both ingredients but estimates the moments more robustly. The price is a second pseudoinverse per iteration, which roughly doubles the solver cost of plain SR.

The norm-constrained step size γt\gamma_{t}, also following MARCH, preserves the update direction and either clips the norm of δ​θt\delta\theta_{t} at C0C_{0},

γt​(∥δ​θt∥)=γ​min⁡(1,C0∥δ​θt∥),\gamma_{t}\big(\lVert\delta\theta_{t}\rVert\big)=\gamma\,\min\left(1,\frac{C_{0}}{\lVert\delta\theta_{t}\rVert}\right)\,, (S18)

or regulates it to a scheduled target ctc_{t},

γt​(∥δ​θt∥)=min⁡(1,ct∥δ​θt∥),ct=C01+max⁡(t−t0,0)/T,\gamma_{t}\big(\lVert\delta\theta_{t}\rVert\big)=\min\left(1,\frac{c_{t}}{\lVert\delta\theta_{t}\rVert}\right)\,,\qquad c_{t}=\frac{C_{0}}{1+\max(t-t_{0},0)/T}\,, (S19)

which the raw step norm typically exceeds, so that the realized step norm is ctc_{t} itself. We use Eq. (S18) for the NN-fPEPS and Eq. (S19) for the backflows, and observe no significant difference between the two. In the benchmark of Fig. S4 performed on the BCS backflow, AdamSR tolerates a larger C0C_{0} than SPRING and MARCH and converges fastest. Its advantage is even clearer for the NN-fPEPS, which SR, SPRING, and MARCH fail to train to good convergence in our numerical experiments.

B Solving linear equations

Lines 5 and 9 of Algorithm A solve

A​x=b,x=A+​b,Ax=b\,,\qquad x=A^{+}b\,, (S20)

where AA has the Ns×NpN_{s}\times N_{p} shape of O¯\bar{O}, is distributed across NdN_{d} devices along the sample axis, and is given in single precision together with bb. Since Ns≪NpN_{s}\ll N_{p}, Eq. (S20) is consistent and massively underdetermined. We compare three solvers. The Cholesky solver evaluates the minimum-step SR (MinSR) solution [15, 71], which inverts the kernel in sample space by a Cholesky factorization,

x=A†​(A​A†+λ​𝟙)−1​b.x=A^{\dagger}\left(AA^{\dagger}+\lambda\openone\right)^{-1}b\,. (S21)

The conjugate gradient (CG) method [75, 63, 86] solves the normal equation

A†​A​x=A†​bA^{\dagger}A\,x=A^{\dagger}b (S22)

through the products A†​(A​v)A^{\dagger}(Av). The least-squares minimal residual (LSMR) method [28], as implemented in lineax [70], is a Krylov iteration on Eq. (S20) itself through the Golub–Kahan bidiagonalization of AA (which reduces AA to bidiagonal form, i.e., nonzero only on the diagonal and first subdiagonal). Neither Krylov solver carries a diagonal shift. Starting from x=0x=0, both approach the minimum-norm solution within a Krylov space that grows by one direction per iteration, so the stopping criterion alone sets the accuracy and acts as the regularizer [39].

The Cholesky solver relies on a matrix factorization, whereas CG and LSMR are iterative, and the two classes differ in three respects.

  • •

    Precision. The Cholesky solver forms A​A†AA^{\dagger}, whose condition number is the square of that of AA, and therefore needs double precision (FP64). Both Krylov solvers run in single precision (FP32), where the error floor is set by accumulating the matrix–vector products over NpN_{p} terms, ϵ32​Np∼10−4\epsilon_{32}\sqrt{N_{p}}\sim 10^{-4} for the FP32 machine epsilon ϵ32≈1.2×10−7\epsilon_{32}\approx 1.2\times 10^{-7}, rather than by the squared condition number. This also suits hardware with reduced or no double-precision throughput, such as the NVIDIA B300 GPU and Google TPUs.

  • •

    Parallelism. A Krylov iteration accesses AA only through A​vAv and A†​uA^{\dagger}u, so it distributes over many nodes with a fixed memory footprint per device. The factorization needs the whole Ns×NsN_{s}\times N_{s} kernel, which is either replicated on every device or factorized across devices at a substantial communication cost, as in JAXMg [84].

  • •

    Accuracy. The cost of a factorization does not depend on the shift, so the Cholesky solver reaches an arbitrarily small residual simply by lowering λ\lambda. A Krylov solver can only approach its target by adding iterations.

Fig. S5 compares the three solvers in wall-clock time, in-sample residual η=∥A​x−b∥/∥b∥\eta=\lVert Ax-b\rVert/\lVert b\rVert, and step norm ∥x∥\lVert x\rVert. For the Pfaffian backflow with Np≈1.2N_{p}\approx 1.2M, the Cholesky solver is four to six times faster than the Krylov solvers at every NsN_{s} where its kernel fits in memory, even though it reaches a ten times smaller residual. This is because the spectrum of A​A†AA^{\dagger} decays quickly for the Pfaffian backflow state, so the Krylov solvers need more iterations (six to eight times more iterations than for the NN-fPEPS). For the NN-fPEPS with the larger Np≈4.6N_{p}\approx 4.6M, the Cholesky solver is faster up to Ns=4096N_{s}=4096, and the Krylov solvers take over from Ns≈8×103N_{s}\approx 8\times 10^{3} on. At the same number of iterations, LSMR leaves a residual 1.31.3 times that of CG but returns a step norm 1.11.1 times smaller, indicating less overfitting to the finite sample, at nearly the same time cost.

These results suggest choosing the solver by the network size and the degree of parallelism. The Cholesky solver is the better choice for networks with up to a few million parameters trained on a small number of GPUs, where the Ns×NsN_{s}\times N_{s} kernel fits in device memory and its factorization remains cheap. CG and LSMR are better suited to larger networks distributed over many GPUs, where NsN_{s} grows with the number of devices and the factorization becomes prohibitive in both cost and memory, while each Krylov iteration only requires matrix–vector products that parallelize across devices with modest communication. In this work, we therefore use LSMR for the large-scale parallel simulations of the NN-fPEPS and the Cholesky solver in all other cases.

C Hyperparameters and details

For completeness, we collect here the settings shared by most production runs of this work.

  • •

    Sampling. We employ a mixed sampler that proposes an electron hopping or a neighbor-site exchange with equal probability. The total number of samples is Ns=8192N_{s}=8192. Each VMC iteration includes 2​N2N MCMC steps for system sizes up to 24×2424\times 24, and 4​N4N MCMC steps for the 32×3232\times 32 lattice.

  • •

    Energy clipping. For robustness against heavy-tailed fluctuations, the local energies entering ϵ¯\bar{\epsilon} are clipped to ⟨Eloc⟩±5​σ\left<E_{\mathrm{loc}}\right>\pm 5\sigma, with σ2\sigma^{2} the sampled energy variance [36], while the reported energy and variance are unclipped.

  • •

    Optimizer. In AdamSR, μ=0.95\mu=0.95 and β=0.995\beta=0.995. The NN-fPEPS runs adopt the clipped step size of Eq. (S18) with C0=200C_{0}=200 and the learning rate γ=max⁡(2.56/N,10−3)\gamma=\max(2.56/N,10^{-3}), while the backflow runs adopt the scheduled step norm of Eq. (S19) with C0=1C_{0}=1, reduced to C0=0.5C_{0}=0.5 in most runs continued from trained weights, t0=1000t_{0}=1000, and T=4000T=4000.

  • •

    Linear solver. When the Cholesky solver is used, the diagonal shift is λ=10−6\lambda=10^{-6} for the NN-fPEPS and λ=10−3\lambda=10^{-3} for the backflows. When LSMR is used, the relative tolerance passed to lineax is 10−410^{-4}.

  • •

    Numerical precision. The Cholesky solver uses FP64, and the HOTRG steps and the LSMR solver use FP32 without TF32. Other computations are performed in FP32 with TF32 employed whenever possible.

  • •

    Weight transfer. The NN-fPEPS is first trained on the 16×416\times 4 lattice (t′=0t^{\prime}=0) or the 8×88\times 8 lattice (t′=−0.2t^{\prime}=-0.2). For larger systems, the trained weights are transferred from smaller systems in the following order—16×4/ 8×8→16×8→16×16→32×3216\times 4\,/\,8\times 8\rightarrow 16\times 8\rightarrow 16\times 16\rightarrow 32\times 32. Backflows are cold-started at 16×1616\times 16, and then transferred to 24×2424\times 24 and 32×3232\times 32.

  • •

    Total iterations. On the 16×1616\times 16 lattice, each state is trained for ∼5000\sim 5000 steps with translation symmetry but without the symmetry projection of Eq. (S16), followed by another ∼1000\sim 1000–50005000 steps with the projection. On the 32×3232\times 32 lattice, this is reduced to ∼1000\sim 1000 steps without projection and ∼300\sim 300–10001000 steps with projection.

V Time cost

All times are measured on NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPUs, at batch sizes that saturate the GPU, on the Perlmutter supercomputer at the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC) with 4 GPUs per node, except for the determinant and Pfaffian rows of Table S3, which are taken from the benchmarks of the fermix library [18] on the same GPU model. The efficiency is quoted as the model FLOPs utilization

MFU=Ft​P,\mathrm{MFU}=\frac{F}{t\,P}\,, (S23)

with FF the number of floating-point operations executed by the timed implementation, tt the wall-clock time, and PP the A100 peak throughput, 156156, 19.519.5, and 5252 TFLOP/s for TF32, FP32, and 3×\timesTF32, the emulation of FP32 matrix products by three TF32 products. For rows that mix several arithmetic types, t​Pt\,P is replaced by the sum of ti​Pit_{i}P_{i} over the parts.

A Amplitude evaluation

Table S3 and Fig. S6 give the cost of one evaluation of each component of the ansatzes on a single GPU. An NN-fPEPS amplitude combines the bottleneck CNN with the fPEPS (trans), with comparable shares at every size. A Pfaffian backflow amplitude combines the normal CNN with the Pfaffian, apart from the untimed assembly of the pairing matrix, and is dominated by the normal CNN up to 16×1616\times 16 and by the Pfaffian from 32×3232\times 32 on. The determinant and Pfaffian rows use our batched GPU kernels for the blocked LU and Parlett–Reid factorizations of the fermix library [18]. All rows are measured at half filling.

B VMC step

Fig. S7 shows the weak and strong scaling of one optimization step of the 16×1616\times 16 NN-fPEPS production runs at U=8U=8 and t′=−0.2t^{\prime}=-0.2. A step consists of one sweep of 2​N2N Metropolis updates per sample, the local energies with about 2​N2N amplitudes ψ⁡(n′)\psi(n^{\prime}) per sample, and the Jacobian at twice the cost of a forward pass, all evaluated with the 88 elements of the symmetry group PP in one call. The number of LSMR iterations is fixed at 100100 for a direct comparison, although it may need to grow with NsN_{s} to keep the residual error η\eta unchanged. The tests stop at 512512 GPUs due to the limited number of A100-80GB nodes on Perlmutter. The 10241024-GPU runs in this work use A100-40GB nodes.

VI Pure fPEPS reference

We estimate the exact ground-state energy of the 16×1616\times 16 PBC lattice at t′=0t^{\prime}=0 with pure fPEPS optimized by simple update (SU) [45, 87], evaluated by contracting finite clusters embedded in a belief-propagation environment, and extrapolated to infinite bond dimension.

A Simple update and cluster contraction

The fPEPS use the local fermionic encoding [37, 62, 30] with U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry [76, 77, 8]. The initial product state is a period-88 stripe, with antiferromagnetic order on columns 11–77 and 99–1515, a π\pi phase shift between the two domains, and empty columns 88 and 1616 that hold the 3232 holes of 1/81/8 doping. We first converge SU at bond dimension D=6D=6 and then continue from this state directly at each target bond dimension D=8,10,12,14,16D=8,10,12,14,16. All runs use a second-order Trotter decomposition with the imaginary time step τ=0.5D−3/2\tau=0.5D^{-3/2}. All calculations are performed on CPUs with quimb [33] and the symmray array backend [34].

To evaluate observables of the SU states on the torus, we first gauge each state by running SU without applying any gates, which is equivalent to belief propagation (BP) [2, 83]. This yields a bond weight λb\lambda_{b} on each of the Nb=2​L2=512N_{b}=2L^{2}=512 bonds, shown in Fig. S8(a)–(b).

For each nearest-neighbor term, acting on sites (i,j)(i,j) and (i,j+1)(i,j+1) or (i,j)(i,j) and (i+1,j)(i+1,j), we build a rectangular cluster that extends rr sites in every direction from the two target sites. A horizontal term thus has a Cx×Cy=4×3C_{x}\times C_{y}=4\times 3 cluster at r=1r=1 and a 16×1516\times 15 cluster, which covers nearly the whole lattice, at the largest radius r=7r=7. We cut the bonds along the cluster boundary and place the weights λb\lambda_{b} on every bond of the cluster, including the dangling bonds at its edges. When the cluster spans the full lattice in one direction, Cx=16C_{x}=16 or Cy=16C_{y}=16, its two far edges meet, and both ends of the cut bond between them carry λb\lambda_{b}. This amounts to approximating the environment beyond the cluster by its BP form. This process is shown in Fig. S8(b)–(d).

Each cluster is a PEPS with open boundary conditions, which we partially trace by boundary contraction to obtain an approximate reduced density matrix of the two target sites, as shown in Fig. S8(e). The two boundary environments start from the cluster edges parallel to the target bond and sweep inwards, with the ket and bra layers absorbed in two separate steps and the environments compressed to bond dimension χ\chi after each step. Once the two environments are adjacent to the target site column, one environment is compressed with the ket tensors, and the other with the bra tensors. See Fig. S8(f)–(i). The compression is a variant of successive deterministic compression [60]. A sketching sweep with randomized low-rank SVDs first compresses the environment to the oversampled bond dimension 1.5​χ1.5\chi, truncating every charge sector in proportion, and a final direct SVD then truncates it to χ\chi by ranking the singular values across all charge sectors. The contraction thus costs 𝒪⁡(D3​χ3)\mathcal{O}(D^{3}\chi^{3}), remains accurate, and is compatible with U⁡(1)U(1) fermionic tensor networks. Each reduced density matrix is normalized individually.

The results for the energy per site, E/NE/N, as a function of DD, rr, and χ\chi are shown in Fig. S9. We also show the energies calculated by full boundary contraction, i.e., without the cluster approximation. These are more expensive to compute, with a cost of 𝒪⁡(D5​χ3)\mathcal{O}(D^{5}\chi^{3}), and converge more noisily, so we do not use them to estimate energies. Nonetheless, they appear to be consistent with the cluster boundary approximation.

B Extrapolation

The procedure above gives the energy per site as a function of the PEPS bond dimension DD, the cluster radius rr, and the boundary bond dimension χ\chi, which we extrapolate by bootstrapping.

For each DD, we fit the energies at the largest radius r=7r=7 and the three largest boundary dimensions χ=192\chi=192, 256256, and 384384 to

E⁡(χ)=E∞+a​χ−p,E(\chi)=E_{\infty}+a\chi^{-p}\,, (S24)

with the exponent p∈{1,2}p\in\{1,2\} drawn at random. The cluster approximation error is accounted for by adding Gaussian noise to E∞E_{\infty} with the standard deviation

σr=|E⁡(r=7,χ=384)−E⁡(r=6,χ=384)|.\sigma_{r}=\left|E(r=7,\chi=384)-E(r=6,\chi=384)\right|\,. (S25)

Individual estimates for E/NE/N at each DD are shown in Figs. S9 and S10. Note that these do not enter the overall bootstrap procedure.

To extrapolate in DD, we use a proxy for the SU discarded weight. The gauge weight of bond bb is the smallest normalized squared singular value

wb=mink⁡λb2​[k]∑kλb2​[k],w_{b}=\frac{\min_{k}\lambda_{b}^{2}[k]}{\sum_{k}\lambda_{b}^{2}[k]}\,, (S26)

where kk runs over the singular values in all charge sectors, and the gauge weight of a state is the geometric mean over all bonds w=(∏bwb)1/Nbw=\left(\prod_{b}w_{b}\right)^{1/N_{b}}. We then extract the energy E0E_{0} from the linear fit

E⁡(w)=E0+c​w.E(w)=E_{0}+c\,w\,. (S27)

Note that the quantity ww and the fitting form here differ slightly from those in, e.g., Ref. [22].

A single bootstrap sample draws pp and the cluster noise for each D=8,10,12,14,16D=8,10,12,14,16, keeps or drops the D=8D=8 point with equal probability, and fits Eq. (S27) to the remaining points. The mean and standard deviation over 10,00010{,}000 bootstrap samples give E/N=−0.7602​(14)E/N=-0.7602(14). Fig. S10 shows this estimate with 100 fitted line samples, and the separate individual estimates for each DD, as a function of ww.

VII Energy benchmarks

A Zero-variance extrapolation

Close to an eigenstate, the energy of a variational state approaches the exact energy linearly in its energy variance, E≈E0+k​σ2E\approx E_{0}+k\sigma^{2} [79, 9]. The states along a VMC optimization therefore fall on a straight line in the (σ2,E)(\sigma^{2},E) plane, whose intercept at σ2=0\sigma^{2}=0 estimates the exact ground-state energy E0E_{0}.

This technique is used to estimate an accurate ground-state energy on the 16×416\times 4 lattice at t′=0t^{\prime}=0 using an NN-fPEPS with Np≈38N_{p}\approx 38M, much larger than that of Table S1. The symmetry projection of Eq. (S16) is also used during training for better accuracy. This state serves only for the extrapolation and the variational energy is not listed in Table S4. We bin the energy and variance of its training curve and fit a straight line by orthogonal distance regression, which accounts for the statistical errors of both (Fig. S11(a)). Repeating the fit over a grid of step windows and bin sizes (Fig. S11(b)), we obtain E0/N=−0.76722​(6)E_{0}/N=-0.76722(6).

B Variational energy

Table S4 lists the variational energies and energy variances of all states in this work, before and after the symmetry projection, together with selected variational energies in existing literature. All our states except the pure fPEPS are translation invariant, and each projected state continues the optimization of the unprojected one under Eq. (S16). The projected energies in Figs. 3(a) and 4(a) of the main text are taken from this table.

VIII Real-space correlations

Figs. S12–S21 show the real-space correlations of all our symmetry-projected states on lattices of 16×1616\times 16 sites and larger, along the two lattice axes. Besides the pair-pair correlation Cp​(r)C_{p}(r) of Eq. (2) of the main text, they include the spin and charge correlations

Cs​(r)=⟨𝑺0⋅𝑺r⟩,Cc​(r)=⟨(n0−n¯)​(nr−n¯)⟩,C_{s}(r)=\langle\bm{S}_{0}\cdot\bm{S}_{r}\rangle\,,\qquad C_{c}(r)=\langle(n_{0}-\bar{n})\,(n_{r}-\bar{n})\rangle\,, (S28)

with n¯=7/8\bar{n}=7/8. To improve visibility of the correlation data, the charge correlation Cc​(r)C_{c}(r) and the pair-pair correlation Cp​(r)C_{p}(r) are multiplied by 5050 and 100100, respectively, to bring them to the same level as the spin correlation Cs​(r)C_{s}(r).

At t′=0t^{\prime}=0, the NN-fPEPS forms a filled stripe with a spin-density wave (SDW) of period 1616 and a charge-density wave (CDW) of period 88, whose spin and charge correlations persist to the largest distance while its pair-pair correlation decays. The BCS and Pfaffian backflow states instead have short-ranged spin and charge correlations and a saturated pair-pair correlation. At t′=−0.2t^{\prime}=-0.2, the Pfaffian backflow and the NN-fPEPS both form a half-filled stripe with an SDW of period 88 and a CDW of period 44, coexisting with a finite pair-pair correlation that becomes weaker when the system size increases. The BCS backflow result at t′=−0.2t^{\prime}=-0.2 is from Ref. [72] instead of this work. As the correlations were not provided in the work, we do not show them here.
